content: This guide acknowledges the contributions of several individuals to its development. Elena Altieri coordinated the drafting and production of the document, while Tom Hundley served as the editor. Specific sections were contributed by Adrian Brown, Geoffrey Cain, Tom Hundley, Annie Kelly, Guilherme Paranaiba Gouveia, and Subhendu Ray. The drafts were reviewed by Kidist Bartolomeos, Marina Carter, Roberto Colombo, Nathalie Draisin, Paul Garwood, Rebecca Ivers, Meleckidzedeck Khayesi, Etienne Krug, Callie Long, Richard Mills, Evelyn Murphy, Victor Pavarino, Margie Peden, Carolyn Robinson, Eugenia Rodriguez, Hala Sakr, Laura Sminkey, Tamitza Toroyan, Joe Weber, and Elena Yurasova. Additional contributions were provided by Catherine Allen, Sarika Bansal, Sandra Damiani, Banung Ou, and Piyush Tewari. Hélène Dufays supported the document’s production, and Elizabeth Heseltine edited the final draft. WHO is not liable for damages arising from its use. This guide is the culmination of four years of work with media professionals on road safety across ten countries. Between 2011 and 2014, WHO engaged with over 1,300 journalists through road safety workshops to enhance their understanding of this complex issue. The goal was to inspire not just more stories but also more comprehensive and compelling narratives about road traffic injuries and their profound impact on lives. Every day, approximately 3,400 people die in road traffic crashes worldwide, with lives altered in mere seconds. While crash events often make the news, the deeper stories—exploring the causes, preventability, and broader implications—are rarely developed. However, road traffic deaths and injuries are preventable. The United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety (2011–2020) highlights effective interventions, particularly from high-income countries, that can change road user behavior, improve infrastructure, and enhance emergency care systems. Efforts are underway to extend these strategies to lowand middle-income countries, where over 90% of road traffic deaths occur amidst rapid motorization. Despite the preventability of these deaths, the knowledge to address them seldom reaches the news. This guide aims to change that by providing journalists with new angles, examples, and expert tips to foster a new era of road safety journalism focused on solutions and saving lives. Dr. Etienne Krug, Director of the Department for Management of Noncommunicable Diseases, Disability, Violence, and Injury Prevention at WHO, emphasizes the importance of this guide for journalists and editors. It aims to deepen their understanding of road safety and help them produce in-depth stories while identifying opportunities to sustain coverage of this critical public health issue. Tom Hundley, Senior Editor at the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, highlights that road traffic fatalities represent a public health crisis of epic proportions. If such statistics were caused by a virus or disease, they would dominate headlines, attract funding, and spark global awareness campaigns. Yet, road traffic deaths are often dismissed as isolated, unavoidable accidents. Journalists, especially in lowand middle-income countries, must recognize that these incidents are not random but part of a larger public health crisis affecting societies as a whole. Road safety reporting requires more than familiarity with statistics; it demands an understanding of the complex interplay of factors leading to fatalities. This guide encourages journalists to tell the bigger story behind road safety. Annie Kelly, an editor and journalist at The Guardian, shares her experience as the commissioning editor for the Global Road Safety in Focus project. Initially unfamiliar with road safety issues, she quickly realized its significance as a global health concern and a barrier to education and poverty alleviation. To make road safety compelling, her team focused on strong news hooks and human-interest angles. For example, they highlighted how South Africa’s road deaths rival its murder rate and how children often lose their lives trying to get to school. They also produced multimedia content, such as a video on Mexico City’s anti-drunk-driving squads and an audio slideshow featuring a Kenyan road safety activist. These efforts aimed to bring road safety into the spotlight and demonstrate its relevance to global development. Geoffrey Cain, a freelance journalist, recounts how he successfully pitched a road safety story to Time magazine. He used a dramatic crash in Cambodia as an entry point to discuss the broader implications of road traffic fatalities. The story resonated because it combined a compelling narrative with a deeper exploration of the issue, illustrating the societal costs of road crashes and the urgent need for action. Guilherme Paranaiba Gouveia, a journalist in Brazil, shares how a road safety workshop transformed his reporting. He began to approach traffic-related fatalities with a focus on their broader implications, comparing them to national tragedies to highlight their magnitude. This shift in perspective helped him produce more impactful stories that challenged the culture of normalizing road deaths. Adrian Brown, a journalist specializing in data journalism, describes his work at BBC News Online, where he used data to create engaging narratives about road traffic deaths. One project involved an interactive map of road fatalities in Great Britain, allowing users to explore detailed information about crashes in their area. Another project followed the London Ambulance Service for a day to illustrate the scale of road incidents. These initiatives combined data visualization with human-interest stories to make road safety reporting more compelling. This guide encourages journalists to view road safety as a critical and multifaceted issue that intersects with global development, public health, and human rights. By telling stories that emphasize the human impact and systemic causes of road traffic fatalities, journalists can raise awareness and drive meaningful change.
